summary:
South Sumatra stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that South Sumatra, alongside Aceh, criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in that province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Reporting on attacks in Bogor, West Java, links that decree to 10 attacks on trans women between 30 March and 15 July 2026, with 45 victim-survivors recorded by an advocacy group; victims were punched, kicked and in some cases stripped. An official quoted in that reporting insists the decree is a broader defence policy not aimed at LGBTQI people.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Within South Sumatra, Palembang's city government is preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, announced by Mayor Ratu Dewa in the Grand Mosque courtyard on 19 July 2026 and presented as local follow-through on the presidential regulation of October 2025 that places the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats in national defence policy for 2025-2029. No penalty is specified in the draft and no enforcement has been documented.

OutRight Action International's 'Creeping Criminalisation' mapping of discriminatory regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces includes South Sumatra, evidencing the province's place in a regional-bylaw belt that drafts like Palembang's extend.
tangentialFactors:
Two regulatory layers operate at once in South Sumatra. National morality provisions apply directly province-wide, while regional bylaws add locally drafted restrictions on LGBT conduct and expression. OutRight Action International's mapping identifies the same pattern in eight provinces, which places South Sumatra inside a wider belt of local regulation rather than an isolated case.

Officials characterise the October 2025 presidential regulation as a general defence measure covering separatism and terrorism alongside LGBTQ+ activity, and an official quoted in August 2026 reporting denied that it targets LGBTQI people. Reporting for the same period nevertheless attributes a documented rise in attacks on trans women to that regulation and to official condemnation.

The province's own criminalisation provision sits alongside Aceh's separately imposed religious-law punishments. Aceh's caning sentence of February 2025 is the clearest recent illustration of what religious-law penalties can look like when applied, though they are not enforceable in South Sumatra.

Residents of South Sumatra live under both national morality provisions and the province's own criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Palembang's city government is preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, announced on 19 July 2026; it is in preparation, with no penalty specified and no enforcement documented to date.

Legal gender recognition in Indonesia requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and identity documents recognise only 'male' and 'female' descriptors with no third-gender or X option.

No national law protects residents from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so remedies for workplace, housing or service discrimination are not available under statute. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025, which would further narrow domestic expression and media use.

Police raids on private LGBT gatherings have produced mass arrests; the Puncak villa operation of 22 June 2025 detained 75 people at a gathering that Amnesty International said broke no law. Vigilante violence against trans women has been recorded at scale, with 10 attacks in one city between 30 March and 15 July 2026 and 45 victim-survivors logged by an advocacy group.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Palembang regulation was reported as being in preparation in July 2026. Its text, any penalty it creates and any enforcement under it are unresolved on the available sources.

The attack figures reported in August 2026 for Bogor, West Java (10 attacks between 30 March and 15 July 2026; 45 victim-survivors) are attributed to advocacy-group data and are not independently corroborated in the inventory; their equivalent scale within South Sumatra itself is not sourced.

Whether South Sumatra's own criminalising provision has been applied to foreign visitors, and with what penalties, is not sourced in this inventory. Aceh's use of provincial religious law against visitors is documented; the parallel South Sumatra position is not.

The status of the 2025 bill on online content after the period covered by the sources, and whether any national or provincial anti-discrimination instrument has been drafted, remain unresolved.
